The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
\frac{y}{x}=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2(0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,0)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,0),$ we get

$$
H(1,0)=det({f}^{″}(1,0))=0\cdot (-2)-{1}^{2}=-1<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,0).$
